etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English plot, plotte, from Old English plot (“a plot of ground”), from Proto-Germanic *plataz, *platjaz (“a patch”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Middle Low German plet (“patch, strip of cloth, rags”), German Bletz (“rags, bits, strip of land”), Gothic 𐍀𐌻𐌰𐍄𐍃 (plats, “a patch, rags”). See also plat. See also complot for an influence on or source of sense 5.

Sense 9 is a back-formation from for the plot.

definitions.definition: (narratology) The course of a story, comprising a series of incidents which are gradually unfolded, sometimes by unexpected means. [from 1640s]

quote.citation: c. 1725, Alexander Pope, View of the Epic Poem:
quote.text: If the plot or intrigue must be natural, and such as springs from the subject, then the winding up of the plot must be a probable consequence of all that went before.

definitions.definition: An area or land used for building on or planting on. [from 1550s]
A graph or diagram drawn by hand or produced by a mechanical or electronic device.

quote.citation: 2017, Mark Chambers, Tony Holmes, Nakajima B5N ‘Kate’ and B6N ‘Jill’ Units, page 32:
quote.text: I was told to fly out on a vector of 100 degrees to meet a strong plot of aircraft 30 miles from the coast.

definitions.definition: A secret plan to achieve an end, the end or means usually being illegal or otherwise questionable. [from 1580s]

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene vi]:
quote.text: I have o'erheard a plot of death.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene i, page 1:
quote.text: O, think what anxious moments pass between / The birth of plots and their last fatal periods!

definitions.definition: Contrivance; deep reach thought; ability to plot or intrigue.

quote.citation: a. 1669, John Denham, On Mr Thomas Killigrew's Return from Venice, and Mr William Murrey's from Scotland:

definitions.definition: Participation in any stratagem or conspiracy.

quote.citation: 1644, J[ohn] M[ilton], The Doctrine or Discipline of Divorce: […], 2nd edition, London: [s.n.], →OCLC, book:
quote.text: And when Christ saith, Who marries the divorced commits adultery, it is to be understood, if he had any plot in the divorce.

quote.citation: 1651, Jer[emy] Taylor, The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Francis Ashe […], →OCLC:
quote.text: no other plot in their religion but serve God and save their souls

definitions.definition: (fandom slang, euphemistic) Attractive physical attributes of a fictional character; assets.
(transitive, intransitive) To conceive (a crime, misdeed etc).
(transitive) To trace out (a graph or diagram).
(transitive) To mark (a point on a graph, chart, etc).

quote.text: This treatise plotteth down Cornwall as it now standeth.
